transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-21
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 39 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Miller (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Ari Chen (Tempest Head of ML), Samira Ortiz (Tempest Platform Eng), Liam Park (Tempest CTO)

Summary (auto): Weekly POC check-in focused on economics after enabling prefix caching and adjusting batch sizes. Went over early numbers and next steps.

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Jordan (Redwood AE): hey everyone, thanks for joining. i see we have ari, samira, liam — thanks for making time. we'll run quick through the numbers priya pulled, then decisions and next steps.
[00:18] Ari (Tempest): yeah thanks jordan. sorry i've got a kid in the background so if i drop it's ok.
[00:24] Priya (Redwood SE): no problem, we can keep this to 40. quick note: transcription may have small errors, i saw kv cache turned into k v cash in the draft so ignore weird words.
[00:38] Samira (Tempest): ha, yes that happened last week. ok priya, numbers?
[00:43] Priya: alright, i ran the micro-bench yesterday. baseline (no prefix cache, batch=1) with the open-llama-16b-ish variant we onboarded gave ~2.1 tokens/sec per GPU at ~0.045 tokens per dollar (this is us normalizing to your pilot infra costs). after enabling prefix KV cache (we saw ~38-42% cold->warm hit within the 95th prompts) tokens/sec effective rose to 3.6 and tokens/sec per dollar improved by roughly 60%.
[01:20] Ari: when you say hit rate 38-42, is that on real traffic mix or synthetic?
[01:26] Priya: this was on the 1k sample set you initially gave us — the "pilot sample". we suspect in production your hit rate will be higher because many prompts share prefixes, but we wanted conservative numbers.
[01:38] Liam: can you remind us the latency impact? our 95th P90 is fairly strict, 300 ms for UI paths.
[01:46] Priya: good question. cold-start latency is unchanged, warm requests saw a 12-18% reduction in p95 tail because the KV cache keeps KV contexts off the critical path. but batching increases median throughput at the expense of tail — at batch=8 we saw median token gen latency drop, but p95 moved up by ~70 ms in our infra. so it's a tradeoff.
[02:10] Jordan: important to call out tokens/sec/$ is a function of batch sizes and cache hit rate, and also quantization. priya, we briefly tried 4-bit quant, results?
[02:20] Priya: yes, 4-bit (we used the q4_0 like profile) improved tokens/sec by ~1.9x on the same device but introduced minor quality diffs on long-context prompts — some hallucination on very precise code outputs. for customer workflows that are tolerant (e.g., chat suggestions) it's fine; for code-gen or legal text you'd want to validate with the eval set. cost improved roughly 55% in tokens-per-dollar when combining quant + cache.
[02:52] Ari: interesting. what about dedicated vs hosted — if we go dedicated GPUs with reserved capacity does the econ look better?
[02:59] Jordan: yes reserved dedicated improves unit cost predictability; for high sustained throughput it usually beats hosted per-token price after you hit commit thresholds. but you lose the elasticity — that's where our fallback routing helps (hosted fallback during spikes).
[03:17] Samira: can fallback route preserve prefix cache? i.e., if requests go to hosted during burst, do we lose cache benefits?
[03:24] Priya: currently prefix cache is per-runtime. cross-region or cross-deployment cache sharing is possible with a shared K-V store but there is added complexity and egress costs. short answer: you may lose some hit rate on immediate fallback. we can demo a shared cache config though.
[03:40] Ari: ok makes sense.
[03:44] [04:00] Jordan: let's pull up slide 3 from the shared deck — the pilot cost scenarios. (link in chat: /redwood/pilot-pricing-tempest-v2.pdf)
[04:09] Priya: the conservative scenario (no quant, batch=1) landed you at about ~$0.14 per 1k tokens; with caching+batch 8 + q4 we model $0.05 per 1k tokens. those are illustrative and assume a 55% cache hit and sustained QPS as in our sample.
[04:32] Liam: how sensitive is that to cache hit rate? if hit drops to 25% does the cost jump significantly?
[04:38] Priya: yes — we included a sensitivity table. at 25% hit the tokens-per-dollar improvement falls to ~28% vs baseline. at 60% hit you get ~72% improvement. so it's non-linear.
[04:55] Ari: how about batching policies — we have very bursty traffic. bigger batches give efficiency but hurt latency. any hybrid suggestions?
[05:04] Priya: for bursty patterns we recommend dynamic batching + deadline-aware scheduling. Redwood's runtime supports per-route latency targets; you can set a max batching window (e.g., 25ms) and a target batch size. that gives you most of the batching benefit without blowing up p95. in our test we used adaptive windows so that 70% of requests hit batch sizes 2-4 and only heavy loads make it to 8.
[05:30] Samira: is the adaptive batching part of hosted by default or extra config?
[05:34] Jordan: it's built in but you need to set route-level policies in the console; Priya can share recommended templates.
[05:41] Priya: i'll drop the template. also note we can set per-customer SLO overrides and fallback policies for critical paths.
[05:52] [06:10] Ari: on the model variants, you mentioned open-llama-ish 16b and smaller 7b. what's the recommended split?
[06:18] Priya: typical pattern: cheaper 7b variants for routine completions, 16b for heavier reasoning. you can route by prompt classification or confidence score. that reduces cost and keeps latency tight. in our pilot run, using 7b for 60% of requests plus caching gave a 30% additional cost saving vs single-model 16b.
[06:40] Liam: is model switching causing context retransmission overhead?
[06:44] Priya: a little. if you route mid-conversation and need full context on a different variant you might re-send some tokens — that's where prefix caching helps because the new runtime can warm keys faster.
[06:56] Ari: any security/reg concerns with caching? like PII in cache?
[07:01] Jordan: good callout. cache policies can be configured to strip sensitive tokens, and Redwood supports per-route retention TTLs plus encrypted KMS-backed storage. we'll share the security appendix.
[07:15] Samira: perfect, please send SOC2 docs again.
[07:18] Jordan: will do, with the pilot pricing note.
[07:23] [08:00] Priya: quick note on measurement: we are reporting tokens/sec/$ normalized to your cloud cost model which for Tempest is a blended GPU hour cost you shared. if that cost changes our numbers shift linearly. also we measured 'tokens per GPU second' and then converted.
[08:42] Ari: i noticed the earlier bench had strange transcriptions where they spelled caches as cash. haha.
[08:46] Priya: yep i mentioned that.
[08:50] [09:00] Liam: on the benchmark you ran, did you include memory pressure scenarios where several large contexts are active? that was our main worry — memory thrash hurting throughput.
[09:10] Priya: yes we included a 'heavy context' test: 8 concurrent long-context requests with batch=4 and we saw a 12% throughput drop vs ideal; for 16-concurrent it was 24%. that's where quantization helps — lower memory footprint reduces thrash.
[09:33] Ari: what's your recommended quant + cache baseline for our use case?
[09:37] Priya: i'd recommend q4 for most paths + prefix caching enabled + adaptive batch target 4 with 25ms max window. run the 24-hour sim with your traffic mix — that will show real hit rate and enough diurnal variance.
[09:50] Jordan: we're proposing a short 24-hour benchmark run — Priya will execute on Redwood infra and on your dedicated test VPC to compare. results will drive next week's recommendations.
[10:02] Samira: for the dedicated test run we'll need the procedure — do you have a checklist?
[10:07] Priya: yes, quick checklist: 1) provide sample prompts, 2) provision test VPC + keys, 3) set pilot routing rules (we can push a template), 4) run 24h with telemetry on caching and request traces, 5) return CSVs and dashboards. i'll attach the checklist.
[10:28] Ari: great.
[10:31] [11:00] Jordan: let's surface a couple of quick risks: 1) quality degradation with aggressive quant, 2) cache privacy concerns, 3) cross-deployment cache consistency when using fallback. We will quantify 1 with the eval set, mitigate 2 with TTLs and scrubbing, and mitigate 3 with fallback policies.
[11:20] Priya: i'll add quality regression alerts to the Optimize pipeline and hook them to your prompt evals.
[11:27] Ari: how about cost visibility during the pilot — can we see tokens/sec/$ in near real time?
[11:32] Jordan: yes console has near-real-time cost per-route; we also export a CSV every hour in the pilot billing bucket. we'll share the export details so samira can pipe into your internal dashboards.
[11:44] Samira: perfect.
[11:46] [12:00] Liam: one more question — competitors popped up in our procurement notes. we had a quick call with Lambda Labs and they said their price was lower for reserved infra. How do you position vs them?
[12:09] Jordan: Lambda often competes on raw infra price; where we differ is the integrated runtime, routing, and observability that reduces ops cost and improves predictability. also our fallback and model-variant rollouts are opinionated so you don't need to build that layer. but we'll include a competitive note for the procurement team.
[12:28] Ari: ok good.
[12:31] [13:00] Priya: ok action items recap: i'll run the 24h bench, jordan will send pricing scenarios, ari shares prompts, samira provisions test vpc. we set the next sync after bench is done.
[13:45] Jordan: final note — expect an email with the pilot pricing PDF, security appendix, and the batching template.
[13:54] Ari: thanks all, sounds good.
[13:56] Samira: thanks team.
[13:57] Jordan: bye everyone.
--- End transcript ---
